youtube.description:
In March 2021, one ship turned sideways in the Suez Canal and hundreds of ships stopped behind it. Real satellite images, archive pictures and maps tell the story of the desert shortcut the world cannot do without.

(Test episode from the automated pipeline.)

paragraphs.text: On the morning of March 23rd, 2021, a ship about as long as the Empire State Building is tall turned sideways in the Suez Canal, and stopped.
This is a real satellite image of it, taken the next day. Four hundred meters of steel, wedged from bank to bank, and nothing could get past.
Astronauts on the International Space Station photographed it too.

shots.photo: File:Ever Given in Suez Canal viewed from ISS.jpg

paragraphs.text: Within days, at least 369 ships were waiting at both ends of the canal, and around 9.6 billion dollars' worth of goods were stuck every single day.

shots.on_screen_text: About $9.6 billion of goods per day

paragraphs.text: So how did a ditch dug through the desert become powerful enough to shake the world economy?
For centuries, ships sailing between Europe and Asia had to go all the way around Africa.
Then a French diplomat, Ferdinand de Lesseps, convinced Egypt's ruler to let him cut a canal straight through the desert.

shots.photo: File:Retrato de Ferdinand de Lesseps, por Felix Nadar.jpg

paragraphs.text: Digging began in 1859. Tens of thousands of Egyptian workers, many of them forced, moved the sand. How many of them died is still disputed.

shots.photo: File:Civil engineering; work on the Suez canal. Wood engraving by Wellcome V0024392.jpg

paragraphs.text: On November 17th, 1869, the canal opened. The sea route from London to the Arabian Sea became almost 9,000 kilometers shorter.

shots.photo: File:L'inauguration du canal de Suez, 17 November 1869 Gal18 riou 001f.jpg

paragraphs.text: But the canal was run by a European company, and in July 1956, Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, took it back.

shots.photo: File:Al-Ahram Newspaper Publish Suez Canal Nationalization.jpg

paragraphs.text: Britain, France and Israel invaded. Within months, pressure from the United States and the Soviet Union forced them to pull out.
In 1967, war closed the canal again, this time for eight years. Fifteen ships were trapped inside. They became known as the Yellow Fleet, after the desert sand that piled up on their decks.
Today, the canal is 193 kilometers long. In 2021 alone, more than 20,000 ships passed through it, carrying about 12 percent of world trade.
On March 29th, after six days, tugs and dredgers finally pulled the Ever Given free.

shots.on_screen_text: 29 March 2021 · hours before it was freed

paragraphs.text: One ship, one week, one narrow ditch in the desert. That is how much the world still depends on the Suez Canal.

shots.subtitle: The shortcut the world runs on
